subagent_summary: With the incumbent hint 2/8 public rollouts scored 1; the six failures all committed early to one reading of the public number, found that reading self-contradictory for a single private value, and then either looped to the token cap (3 of 8 hit the length limit) or emitted a guessed divisor. The revision makes the sum-vs-product role an explicit hidden coordinate of the candidate state and adds the rule that a branch dies only when it fails for every private value, which is exactly the step the wrong rollouts skipped.

All 8 training rollouts were correct, so the incumbent's weakness is transfer (heldout 0.125), not this question: it prescribes the problem-specific substitution w=(z-1)/z and a Mobius image argument rather than a portable rule. The successful rollouts all converged only after reducing to a modulus condition |z-1|=2|z| and completing the square, while the longest ones burned 8k-12.5k tokens enumerating the six roots and fitting a circle through sampled points, hitting self-contradictions; none named the Apollonius circle. One rollout nearly rejected the circle because |z| was not constant, so the revision moves modulus-first to step one, names the Apollonius/perpendicular-bisector dichotomy, and warns that a non-origin-centered circle has varying |z|.

All 8 rollouts framed union = 5 - overlap correctly, but 6 of 6 failures ended with finish_reason=length at the 16384-token cap and the 2 successes only barely finished (~15.5-15.9k tokens), so the failure mode is budget exhaustion, not a wrong setup. The incumbent hint's instruction to parameterize the angle and minimize a piecewise triangle/sector expression drove exactly that: failures looped over trial angles and tangency guesses (30+ 'but how' restarts each, repeated 'too complex to visualize') and never reached a closing computation. The revision replaces the open-ended minimization with a decisive invariance test at the k-fold symmetry center plus an explicit stop condition, which is the step both winners stumbled onto only after heavy flailing.

All 8 public rollouts scored 0 (three ran out of tokens). Every one applied the equal-spacing condition to adjacent board entries, which may come from different polynomials, derived the vacuous contradiction 'a degree-5 polynomial would have to be constant', then guessed a small number (2, 5, 6, 10) or declared the count unbounded. None ever partitioned the indices by which polynomial was chosen, so the per-polynomial root bound and the multiply-by-family-size step never happened; the revised hint forbids the adjacent-difference move explicitly and spells out the grouping, non-degeneracy, product bound, and tightness construction.

7/8 public rollouts were correct; the single failure ran out of tokens after inverting the argument-ratio direction when converting the y-difference of two base-1/2 logs, which produced a negative discriminant. It then spent thousands of tokens re-verifying identical algebra and finally guessed, so the hint now names the base<1 direction trap, adds a cheap ratio sanity-check on the known points, and converts 'no real/in-domain root' into a signal to flip the sign/branch assumption once rather than loop.

All 8 training rollouts scored 0. Five concluded the delivery order is deterministically reversed (answering 1 and 0), and three instead assumed every item is equally likely to be last (answering 1/4), with several also treating the last item delivered as the bottom of the pile rather than the top. The incumbent hint's abstract state-graph advice did not stop these; the revision names the stack push/pop model, states the bottom/top orientation rule, and explicitly rejects both the forced-outcome and equiprobable-path fallacies while keeping the forced-move probability-1 weighting.

All 8 rollouts (0/8) collapsed the same way: they set P(x)=sum a_i x^i and read the rows as P(k)=0, swapping node with exponent, then burned the budget hunting a spurious extra root or chasing the x-coefficient of a Vandermonde product (six hit the 16384-token cap; one concluded a_1=0, another 1/2005). The revised hint forbids that role swap, states explicitly that the unconstrained constant term is why L(p) reads off the top coefficient, and gives a one-node test-polynomial recipe plus a small-case check so the same technique transfers to any moment/weight system.

All 8 public rollouts scored reward 1 (train_i = 1.0), so the training question is saturated and the only headroom is transfer, where the incumbent scores just 9/80. The incumbent's phrasing is bound to this item's surface features ('equal-street layout', 'every listed stage total', 'maximum-feasible-count interpretation'), and rollouts spent long stretches re-litigating that undefined jargon (4-15 restatements plus 6-23 'wait' backtracks each, up to 6928 tokens), so it reads as item-specific scaffolding rather than portable method. I replaced it with the same underlying procedure stated generically - name the hidden count, derive it from integrality/gcd plus structural grouping constraints, state the tie-break assumption, then aggregate-scale-divide and sanity-check - which should carry to unseen problems of this class.

All 8 rollouts scored 0 and 7 of 8 hit the 16384-token cap: every one set up p=ax^3+bx^2+cx-24, q=ex^3+fx^2+gx+30 and tried to match all ten coefficients of the degree-9 composition, then looped on self-contradictions (a^2=a, 3a^2=0) it could not resolve. The incumbent hint gestured vaguely at 'a shared affine coordinate' but never told the student what that coordinate is, so nobody tried a centered ansatz; the revision names the common-fixed-point substitution, gives the leading-coefficient consequence that forces the odd-degree sign flip, and says to recover the center by adding the two supplied values.

Only 2/8 rollouts were correct and five of the six failures hit the token cap while trying to derive an abstract bitwise/affine formula for the composed permutation, exactly what the incumbent hint asks for first. The failures that did terminate asserted cycle structures they never traced (order 2 for the size-4 case, a bogus odd-length cycle for size 8), so the revision front-loads concrete tabulation of one full operation plus an explicit disjoint-cycle lcm step and defers any symbolic formula.

Round-2 rollouts scored 2/8; every wrong rollout read "I don't know" as global ambiguity among all factor pairs, then noticed that a speaker's own number plus one fixed reading pins the partner, declared a contradiction, and substituted an invented tie-breaker about the hidden aggregate's uniqueness (three of eight also burned the token cap looping on that contradiction). The revision names the actual source of residual uncertainty - several readings alive for one private value - and gives a concrete per-value partner-counting rule plus a bar on inventing tie-breakers, which is the exact step the failures skipped.

All 8 rollouts scored 1 and every one reached the modulus ratio within the first few hundred tokens, so training accuracy is saturated and the remaining cost is transfer plus wasted verification: after already completing the square, 6 of 8 rollouts re-derived individual roots from nth roots of unity (11-29 exponential expressions each) and one spent 22 'Wait' hedges questioning whether the locus really held because |z| was not constant. The incumbent fires only on the literal template (z-a)^n=c(z-b)^n and names Apollonius as a label, so the revision keys the trigger on the general goal ('locus of all solutions'), states the modulus mechanism |AB|=|A||B| that generates the ratio, and asserts that a necessary condition already IS the locus so the model stops refitting circles through sampled roots.

Round-2 training hit 7/8 with the incumbent, and every rollout (including the winners) reached a verdict by verbal plausibility rather than by any actual area computation; the single failure talked itself into a 'sides tangent, so overlap is half the small square' claim and reported it without ever clipping a region. Meanwhile heldout fell from 0.175 to 0.0875 under the incumbent, so its narrow k-fold-wedge-tiling criterion is not transferring. This revision keeps the min-overlap framing and the invariance-then-stop control flow but replaces the bespoke symmetry criterion with a portable half-plane/shoelace recipe plus an explicit ban on uncomputed overlap values, and falls back to breakpoint-and-stationary-point search only when sampled values disagree.

My 8 public rollouts with the incumbent hint scored 5/8; all three failures hit the 16384-token cap rather than reaching a wrong answer. One did reach the N x deg-P product but then spent thousands of tokens doubting it as 'too large for a competition' and re-litigating the construction; the other two never partitioned indices by function and looped on the vacuous adjacent-difference contradiction until truncation. The revision therefore keeps the grouping/root-bound skeleton but adds an explicit stop rule: accept the product, justify it once by block-interpolation (free coefficients remain), and terminate instead of re-deriving.

All 8 public rollouts were correct this round (train_i=1.0), so the training question is saturated and the binding constraint is transfer, which fell from 0.15 to 0.1375 when the incumbent grew to 151 tokens. Every rollout's real decision point was not the log-base direction the incumbent warns about but the quadratic yielding two in-domain roots, one of which reproduces a given vertex and collapses the figure; rollouts burned many tokens rediscovering that filter. The revision drops the discriminant flip-and-redo advice and states the portable pipeline: fit parameters, use the displacement to reduce to one unknown, exploit y-shift as a multiplicative argument factor, then reject degenerate and out-of-domain roots before the cross-product area.

All 8 of my public rollouts scored 0 with two recurring errors: four asserted the delivery order is deterministically reversed (answering 1 and 0), and four treated outcomes as uniform over permutations or over which item lands last (answering 1/24 or 1/4). Six also inverted the pile orientation, treating the last item delivered as the bottom rather than the top, which makes the position asked about untestable. The revision therefore states the first-in-is-bottom rule and the position-to-arrival-rank translation explicitly, and replaces the incumbent's abstract state-graph advice with an explicit enumerate-then-weight recipe that names the forced-move weight 1 and bans favorable/total counting.

All 8 rollouts scored 0 with one shared root cause: each recast the unknowns as coefficients of a polynomial evaluated at the row index, swapping the weight index with the condition exponent, then burned the budget (7 of 8 hit the token cap) chasing a phantom extra root or a harmonic-sum coefficient. Two rollouts did construct the small analogue and found it inconsistent or underdetermined, yet read that as their own confusion instead of proof the setup was wrong, so this revision makes the small case an explicit falsification test of the setup and replaces full-system solving with a single-target probe step.

All 8 of my round-2 public rollouts scored reward 1 (train_i = 1.0), so the training item is saturated and the only headroom is transfer, where the incumbent gets 9/80. The wasted effort was not arithmetic but ambiguity churn: each rollout burned 16-29 'wait' backtracks re-arguing whether the listed figures were village totals or per-house amounts and whether the 20 percent markup applied to the total or to the per-unit cost, running 2.7k-6.8k tokens. Round 1 showed that genericizing away the gcd / maximum-feasible-count mechanic costs train (8/8 down to 3/8) for only +2 heldout, so I kept that mechanic and added portable instructions to fix both readings once and to note that a uniform percentage commutes with the division, which should cut backtracking on unseen items of this class.

With the incumbent hint all 8 public rollouts were correct (8/8, avg ~5.2k tokens vs 7 of 8 hitting the 16k cap in round 1), so the training question is saturated and the remaining loss is transfer (heldout 0.1625). Reading the correct rollouts, the one wasted stretch is that each spends many lines re-deriving the B=+-A sign because the hint asserted B=-A without the factored form, and several first restate the full ax^3+bx^2+cx+d setup before recentering. The revision therefore states the general normalize-invariants-then-recenter procedure, gives the factored leading-term condition AB(A^(n-1)-B^(n-1))=0 with an instruction to carry both branches, and widens the trigger from commuting cubics to polynomial functional identities generally so it can transfer.

4/8 correct; all four failures came from mis-tracing the block swap rather than from missing the lcm idea the incumbent already supplies. One rollout produced a non-injective position map (two positions sent to the same target) and never noticed, one asserted the composition of the overlapping swaps was an involution and answered 2, and two burned the token cap guessing closed forms after generating mutually inconsistent per-size counts. The revision therefore replaces abstract index tracing with rewriting a concrete labeled string, adds a per-stage every-label-exactly-once check, and replaces cycle-structure guessing with counting repeats until the string returns.

All 8 round-3 rollouts scored 0: six explicitly argued that a speaker who knows their own number plus the public number can compute the partner, concluded both the sum reading and the product reading are impossible, and then emitted an arbitrary divisor of the public number to fill the answer box (three separate divisors appeared across the eight samples), while three burned the token cap looping on that same contradiction. The revision front-loads an explicit per-speaker knowledge inventory that forbids 'just subtract/divide', replaces group-deletion language with a concrete per-private-value count of partners across readings, and adds an explicit bar on guessing when every reading looks contradictory - the exact point where every failure went astray.

All 8 round-3 rollouts scored 1 (3.3k-7.7k tokens), so training is saturated and the loss is transfer: every rollout got |z-a|=k|z-b| within a few hundred tokens, but then 4 of 8 burned 12-40 exponential expressions re-deriving individual roots to spot-check the locus, and 3 of 8 (including the two most hedged, 16-18 'Wait's) stalled on a self-inflicted contradiction from testing the center point itself and concluding the circle was wrong. The revision therefore adds a portable constant-work route to the circle's data (the two collinear points where the bars drop, which bound a diameter, giving center as midpoint and radius as half the distance), demotes the coordinate expansion to a single cross-check, and states explicitly that the center is not on the circle so |z| varying is expected.

Round-3 training reproduced 7/8 with the incumbent; the single failure never ran the incumbent invariance test properly because it mis-listed the large square vertices and then evaluated the aligned orientation as full containment (overlap = whole small square) instead of the actual corner region, so its two test values disagreed and it settled on a verbally asserted rotated fraction with no computed region. Held-out also fell to 0.0875 under the incumbent, indicating its bespoke k-fold-wedge criterion is being applied by fiat rather than checked, while the round-2 shoelace variant lifted held-out to 0.2 but collapsed train. This revision therefore prepends a cheap coordinate/vertex audit and an explicit ban on uncomputed overlap fractions, keeps the invariance-then-stop control flow that trains well, and routes disagreement back to re-checking the region instead of a costly general clipping search.

My 8 public rollouts scored 6/8; both failures were token-cap truncations, never wrong answers. One never partitioned indices at all and burned the budget building a recursive shift construction from adjacent-term differences; the other quoted the hint's product late but then re-imposed a constant successive difference within a single polynomial's own values, concluded 'each function contributes at most one term', and looped. The revision therefore targets that specific trap: it states that a function's index group need not be consecutive so its own successive differences carry no information, and adds a discard rule for any line ending in 'P must be affine' or 'one term per function'.

Train fell to 5/8 with the incumbent. All three failures shared one root cause: after solving the reduced rational equation they assigned the translated vertex a y-value that does not satisfy the curve (P off the graph), and two of them noticed the contradiction, called the problem inconsistent, and reported the area anyway; the third burned its whole budget on a mis-fit parameter pair it never sanity-checked against the given points. The revision keeps the reduction pipeline but replaces the discriminant flip-and-redo advice with two cheap closures: re-derive the given points' y from the fitted parameters, and evaluate f at every new vertex before any area is computed.

My 8 rollouts under the incumbent scored 2/8; the two successes were the only ones that used the rule 'bottom of the shed is the first bag delivered' and then multiplied 1/2 per real branch point, while five failures assumed uniformity (1/24, 1/4 from 'each bag equally likely to be last') and one inverted the orientation to conclude the outcome was forced. Rounds 1-2 already showed that long enumerate-the-whole-tree hints hurt held-out badly, so this revision stays near the incumbent's length and adds only the two steps the successful rollouts used: translate the asked position into a delivery rank, then count genuine 1/2 branch points versus forced moves.

All 8 rollouts scored 0 with a single shared error: each set P(x)=sum_i a_i x^i and reinterpreted row k as P(k)=0, swapping the node index with the condition exponent; the resulting degree-2005 polynomial with only 2004 roots left one free parameter, so rollouts either stalled declaring the system inconsistent/underdetermined or resolved the free root arbitrarily and reported a harmonic-sum, 1/2005, or 0 value. Rounds 1-2 already tried longer prose warnings against that swap and lost heldout accuracy, so this revision drops the warning framing and instead gives the positive mechanical rule -- apply the rows to a test polynomial evaluated at the nodes, chosen to isolate one weight -- keeping the text near incumbent length since the shorter incumbent transfers best.

All 8 of my round-3 public rollouts scored reward 1 (train_i = 1.0), the third saturated round, so the only headroom is transfer, where the incumbent gets 9/80. Every correct rollout ran the same spine (divide-every-total -> gcd -> take max count -> sum -> scale by 1.2), and their only wasted effort was 6-23 backtracks re-deriving that the gcd is the maximum admissible count and re-reading the domain nouns; rounds 1 and 2 showed that replacing the incumbent with a longer, restructured generic paragraph (137 and 162 tokens) collapses train to 3/8 and 4/8 for only +2 and +3 heldout. So instead of another rewrite I made a minimal-delta edit at nearly the incumbent's length: same sentence skeleton and same operative phrases, but the house/street/construction nouns swapped for domain-neutral ones and the gcd-is-the-largest-N step stated explicitly, which should keep the training spine intact while letting the method apply to non-housing items of this class.

All 8 public rollouts were correct again this round (8/8, 3.8k-6.1k tokens, none truncated), so the training question is saturated and the only loss is transfer and wasted reasoning. Every rollout still burned its first ~800 tokens writing out the generic ax^3+bx^2+cx+d pair before recentering, and each re-derived the B=+-A branch and then argued from scratch about why B=-A, because the incumbent asserts the odd-n sign without a reason. The revision explicitly bans the generic-coefficient opening, supplies the reason (B=A collapses to p=q, which distinct given data forbids), and adds the read-off rule that the fixed point is free and an input at distance d costs only A*d^n, so evaluation needs no expansion; the round-2 attempt to widen the trigger to all polynomial functional identities cost train 5/8, so the p(q)=q(p) trigger is kept concrete.

4/8 correct: one failure asserted the composite of the overlapping block swaps was disjoint transpositions and answered 2 without ever tracing it, and the three length-capped failures thrashed because their position map disagreed with their own string simulation after they silently switched between "slot i receives" and "label at i goes to" (one produced a non-injective map with two positions sent to the same target and never noticed). Two of those reached self-consistent counts for the smallest sizes, then abandoned them and burned the remaining budget inventing piecewise formulas for different n instead of rechecking the smaller simulation.

My 8 public rollouts scored 2/8 and not one of the six failures ever evaluated both readings for a single private value: each opened independent global "case: sum" and "case: product" branches, killed the sum branch by noting a speaker can just subtract, then enumerated only divisors of the public number and emitted an unjustified one (143 twice, 11 once), while three others burned the 16k token cap restarting the same case analysis. The revision converts the incumbent's prose per-value instruction into a concrete single table (rows = candidate private values swept beyond divisors, columns = readings, filled-cell count decides know/don't-know) and adds explicit bars on restarting and on reporting a value with no surviving row, which are exactly the steps the wrong rollouts skipped.

All 8 round-4 rollouts scored 1, so training is saturated and the real loss is transfer; the informative signal is the outlier 14.2k-token rollout that derailed for thousands of tokens on the modulus constant (misapplying |c|^(1/n), trying to absorb the constant into the bracket as (4z)^6, and settling on a wrong k before recovering), plus a 9.4k-token rollout whose first ~40 hedges were the same constant-vs-power confusion. Extracting k is thus the only fragile step in this family, so the revision adds a portable guard (write |c| as a prime power, take the exact nth root, verify k^n = |c|, never fold the constant into the bracket) while keeping the diameter-endpoints shortcut and center-not-on-circle warning that already work.

Round-4 training reproduced 7/8 with the incumbent; the sole failure placed the shared point correctly but then asserted from bounding extents that the small square lay wholly inside the large one, so its aligned test value was the whole small square, its two test orientations disagreed, and it drifted to a verbally guessed rotated fraction. A winning rollout also briefly hit the same containment mistake at the rotated orientation before recovering, so mis-deciding inside/outside is the live failure mode, not the min-overlap framing. Held-out has stayed low (0.0875) under the incumbent's bespoke wedge-tiling wording while earlier shoelace and vertex-audit variants raised held-out but collapsed train, so this revision keeps the invariance-then-stop control flow and adds only a portable rule that a touching corner is a wedge whose membership must come from signed half-plane tests.

My 8 public rollouts with the incumbent hint scored 7/8; the single failure was again a token-cap truncation, not a wrong final answer, and it had already recovered the correct N x deg P bound in its last thousand tokens but never got to box it. That rollout burned most of its budget on degenerate side-cases (can all terms be equal? can a fifth-degree polynomial be constant? is it 1 or 5 terms?) before ever partitioning indices by function. The revision therefore front-loads the partition step, explicitly tells the solver to skip zero-difference / one-term-per-function detours as bound-irrelevant, and replaces the old 'trust the product' line with a commit-and-box-early budget rule.

All 8 public rollouts were correct, so train is saturated and only transfer binds; across rounds heldout has moved inversely with hint length (73 tok -> 0.15, 151 -> 0.1375, 161 -> 0.125, 189 -> 0.075), so this revision is shorter than the incumbent. The three longest rollouts (and the only ones that thrashed or declared the problem contradictory) all wasted thousands of tokens after adding a spurious second closure condition - equating diagonal midpoints or vertex sums - which over-determines the system and forces the new vertices to coincide with the given ones; the short clean rollouts never invoked it and simply carried one free on-curve parameter. The hint therefore names that over-constraint trap explicitly, keeps only the portable reduction lever (y-shift becomes a multiplicative argument factor) plus the degenerate/out-of-domain root filter, and drops the narrow base-under-one and discriminant-flip advice.

All 8 of my public rollouts scored 0 under the incumbent: four asserted the delivery order is deterministically reversed (answering 1 and 0), three assumed uniformity (1/24, or 1/4 from 'each item equally likely to be last'), and one blew its token budget on unstructured case-by-case enumeration. Six also inverted orientation, equating the bottom of the destination pile with the last item delivered rather than the first. The revision therefore front-loads a cheap variability probe (exhibit two sequences with different outcomes) to kill the forced-outcome claim that dominated this round, then states the last-in-on-top rule and the 1/2-versus-forced branch weighting, while staying short since rounds 1-2 showed long enumerate-the-whole-tree hints hurt held-out.

All 8 rollouts scored 0 (7 hit the 16384-token cap) with one shared root cause: each set P(x)=sum_i a_i x^i and reread equation k as P(k)=0, transposing the unknown's index with the condition's exponent; the resulting degree-2005 polynomial with only 2004 roots left a free linear factor, so rollouts stalled calling the system inconsistent/underdetermined or resolved it arbitrarily and reported 1/2005, 0, a harmonic sum, or 1/4008. Rounds 1-3 lost heldout accuracy with long jargon-heavy warnings against the transpose, so this revision instead states the technique jointly as a concrete operation the student can execute -- take your own weighted combination of the equations, which forces evaluation at the listed values and makes the allowed exponent span explicit -- and jointly caps effort by isolating one unknown and evaluating rather than expanding.

All 8 of my round-4 public rollouts scored reward 1 (train_i = 1.0), the fourth saturated round, so the only headroom is transfer, where the incumbent sits at 9/80. Every rollout ran the same spine (each total divisible by N -> gcd -> take it as the count -> sum -> scale by 1.2) with 6-23 'wait' backtracks spent re-litigating the vacuous 'equal-street layout constrains N arithmetically' clause and the total-versus-per-unit reading. Comparing rejected rounds, the two generic rewrites (train 3/8 and 4/8) both made the max-count choice conditional ('if the wording asks for the maximum feasible count'), while the incumbent and the noun-swap round (8/8, 7/8) assert it flatly, so I kept that assertion unconditional while replacing the vacuous grouping clause with the portable rule that group wording only imposes a multiple constraint, and stated the total-versus-per-unit reading is fixed once.

All 8 public rollouts were correct again (8/8, 3.8k-6.1k tokens, none truncated), so the training question is saturated under the incumbent and the entire remaining loss is transfer (heldout 0.1625). Round 2 showed that rewriting the concrete p(q)=q(p) trigger into abstract normalize-invariants language raises heldout slightly but costs train 5/8, and round 3 showed that piling on ansatz-specific micro-detail (generic-setup ban, centered read-off rule) drops heldout to 0.1125, so this revision keeps the proven centered-fixed-point spine almost intact and jettisons only the assertive odd-n sign claim in favor of a jointly-derived reason plus an explicit jettison-test fallback, which should stop unseen problems from being forced into an ansatz that does not fit their data.

3/8 correct with the incumbent; every failure came from re-simulating the whole state for the 2nd, 3rd and 4th applications, accumulating block-swap slips until the student concluded the word oscillates and never returns, or from asserting the composite is disjoint transpositions of order 2 without tracing any cycle. Four of five failures also hit the token cap thrashing between mutually inconsistent per-size counts, so the revision confines hand simulation to a single operation, extracts the permutation once, and moves all repetition into cheap cycle iteration plus lcm.

My 8 public rollouts scored 2/8 (execution 149.97); all six failures enumerated the divisor pairs of the public number but never fed Sasha's announcement back as a constraint on Masha's candidate partners, so they collapsed to a single reading, declared "the partner is uniquely determined, contradiction", and emitted an unjustified divisor (143 three times, 11 once) while two burned the token cap looping on that contradiction. The revision keeps the two-candidates-per-private-value counting rule but adds the missing mechanism explicitly: turn the earlier announcement into a set of admissible partner values and re-count each later speaker's candidates only within that set.

All 8 round-5 rollouts scored 1, so training is saturated and the loss is transfer plus wasted tokens. The dominant failure was the incumbent's compressed modulus line: rollouts wrote |z-a|^n = |c|^(1/n)|z-b|^n (mixing the power and the root in one step) and then carried a wrong ratio for thousands of tokens before self-correcting, with the two longest rollouts (12.2k and 7.0k tokens, 37 and 35 hedges) spending most of their length on that constant. A second sink is that the incumbent gives only a procedure for the circle, so rollouts re-derived the midpoint/half-distance from scratch or ran a full x+iy completion of the square as well; the revision splits the modulus into two explicit steps and supplies closed-form center and radius so the circle step is a substitution.

Round-5 training with the incumbent fell to 4/8, and all four failures share one root cause: the invariance check is run as two independently guessed sample orientations, so a botched rotated-case value (one rollout got a single-point overlap and answered 5, another got a whole-shape overlap, a third got a value disagreeing with the aligned case) either ends the rollout wrong or triggers an open-ended piecewise search that ran out the 16384-token budget in three of eight. Winners instead trusted the aligned computation and argued invariance directly. This revision replaces sample-and-compare with an explicit one-line rotation-symmetry proof (rotating by 2*pi/k maps S to itself and permutes the k wedge positions, partitioning S into k equal pieces) plus a hard floor rejecting single-point and full-containment overlaps, so the student never needs a second computed orientation to commit.

My 8 public rollouts scored 5/8 and, unlike earlier rounds, all three failures terminated normally with wrong answers rather than truncating. Two derived a correct per-function root bound but then reported that cap as the final count instead of summing over the N functions, and one of those used the interpolation count deg P + 1 rather than the root count deg P; the third never used the root bound and assumed each function contributes exactly one index. The revision therefore fixes the cap to the root count and adds an explicit aggregation step plus reject-rules for the two observed off-by-a-factor endings.

All 8 public rollouts were correct (train_i=1.0), so train is saturated and only transfer binds; heldout has tracked hint length inversely across rounds (73 tok -> 0.15, 151 -> 0.1375, 161 -> 0.125, 189 -> 0.075), so this revision is shorter than the 151-token incumbent. The three longest correct rollouts thrashed on hundreds of midpoint/vertex-sum lines and contradiction talk after adding a redundant second closure condition, while the short clean rollouts carried one on-curve parameter; historical failures on this hint instead assigned the translated vertex a y from the carried shift rather than from f, got a point off the graph, and reported an area anyway. The hint keeps only the portable pipeline plus those two cheap guards and drops the narrow discriminant-flip and exponential-form verbosity.

My 8 public rollouts scored 0/8 in two clusters: four asserted the delivery order is deterministically reversed, and three assumed uniformity (one answer per permutation, or per which item lands last); one exhausted its token budget on unstructured enumeration. Rounds 1-4 showed that longer enumerate-the-tree hints all cost held-out relative to the 83-token incumbent, so this revision stays short and swaps the abstract state-graph advice for one portable structural fact: an output order corresponds to a unique legal push/pop word, which simultaneously refutes the forced-outcome and equiprobable-permutation fallacies and reduces the task to pricing that word by its free-versus-forced moves.

All 8 rollouts scored 0 (7 hit the 16384-token cap): every one reinterpreted the rows as a polynomial in the condition number rather than the node, producing a degree-2005 polynomial with only 2004 roots, then spent the budget resolving the phantom free root and reported 1/2005, 0, or a harmonic sum. Two rollouts built a small analogue but gave it more conditions than unknowns, so the toy came out inconsistent and they abandoned the correct framing. This revision keeps the incumbent's proven functional opening and adds the two missing mechanical steps: absorb one node power into each weight so the annihilated exponents start at degree 0 (which is why the functional reads off a top coefficient), and scale the toy's condition count with its unknown count.

5/8 public rollouts were correct; all three failures shared one mode, and it was not arithmetic: they read the stated number of equal groups as the unit count, divided every listed total by it, saw each quotient come out whole, and treated that successful divisibility check as confirmation, so they never ran the gcd/maximum-admissible-count step at all. The incumbent already warns that group wording only imposes a multiple constraint, but it sits mid-paragraph after the gcd sentence and was missed. I front-loaded that warning and added the portable closing of the loophole, namely that divisibility is necessary but not sufficient because every divisor of the gcd also passes, so one must continue to the maximum.

All 8 public rollouts were correct again (8/8, 4.4k-6.0k tokens, none truncated), so the training question stays saturated and every remaining point is transfer; the one visible waste is that some rollouts burned ~3k tokens looping on the algebra of AB^n=BA^n (repeatedly mis-cancelling before recovering B=+-A) and others accepted B=-A purely on the hint's authority. Across rounds only the round-2 proposal raised heldout (0.175), and its distinctive ingredient was the factored condition AB(A^(n-1)-B^(n-1))=0 with an instruction to carry both branches and let data eliminate one, while its train loss came from abstracting the trigger and dropping the fixed-point/verify steps. This revision therefore keeps the incumbent's concrete p(q)=q(p) trigger, centered ansatz, and verification spine untouched and swaps only the asserted odd-n sign for that factored both-branch derivation, so unseen problems whose data favours the B=A branch are not forced into a sign flip.
